query: Using the reported HfZrTiTa0.53 refractory high-entropy alloy as the starting material and its quasi-static properties—786 MPa yield strength, 1314 MPa compressive strength, and 13.5% fracture strain—as the baseline, what single testable hypothesis proposes an intervention to overcome limited strain hardening, poor uniform deformability, and rapid failure as strain rate increases under adiabatic dynamic deformation? Specify the intervention and mechanism, predict changes relative to the baseline in strength, uniform deformation, localization resistance, and impact-induced energy release, define the strain-rate and loading conditions over which the prediction applies, cite supporting evidence from the reported refractory-alloy literature, and describe a matched baseline-versus-intervention experiment that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a controlled warm deformation followed by rapid quenching to the HfZrTiTa0.53 refractory HEA to induce a bimodal grain structure will enhance strain hardening and improve uniform deformability, thereby delaying the onset of adiabatic shear localization and reducing rapid failure at high strain rates during dynamic deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: HfZrTiTa0.53 refractory HEA with quasi‐static yield strength of 786 MPa, compressive strength of 1314 MPa, and fracture strain of 13.5%, likely featuring a relatively coarse and uniform grain structure.
generation.intervention: Thermomechanical treatment consisting of warm deformation at an elevated but controlled temperature followed by rapid quenching to refine grain size distribution and create a bimodal microstructure.
generation.conditions: Dynamic adiabatic deformation tests (e.g., using a split-Hopkinson pressure bar) at strain rates ranging from 10^3 to 10^4 s⁻¹ under ambient conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined bimodal grain structure with a mixed population of fine and coarse grains that enhances grain boundary strengthening and retards dynamic recrystallization and shear band formation.
generation.mechanism: The bimodal structure promotes enhanced strain hardening via increased grain boundary obstacles and supports more uniform plastic flow. This microstructural refinement delays thermal softening and the development of localized deformation (adiabatic shear bands) during rapid loading, thereby improving the alloy’s resistance to dynamic failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline, the treated alloy is expected to exhibit increased dynamic yield strength, a greater uniform deformation range (i.e., higher strains before localization), enhanced resistance to adiabatic shear band formation, and more controlled impact-induced energy release (indicative of higher energy absorption capacity).
generation.baseline: Quasi-static properties of the original alloy (786 MPa yield strength, 1314 MPa compressive strength, 13.5% fracture strain) with known limitations in strain hardening and rapid failure under high strain-rate conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies under high strain-rate dynamic loading (10^3–10^4 s⁻¹) at ambient temperature; its effectiveness may vary outside these conditions or under different loading modes (e.g., tensile vs. compressive).
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of improvements in strength, uniform ductility, and impact energy absorption is uncertain and may depend on the optimization of the processing parameters (temperature, deformation level, quenching rate) as well as the inherent stability of the refractory HEA microstructure under extreme conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy samples: one group as-cast (baseline) and one group subjected to warm deformation followed by rapid quenching to produce a bimodal grain structure. Conduct dynamic compression tests using a split-Hopkinson pressure bar at strain rates from 10^3 to 10^4 s⁻¹ under ambient conditions. Compare mechanical performance (yield strength, uniform elongation, and impact energy absorption) and microstructural evolution (grain size distribution, incidence of adiabatic shear bands) between the two groups.
measurements: Dynamic yield strength and ultimate strength
Energy absorption or impact-induced energy release
Microstructural analyses (grain size distribution via TEM/EBSD and quantification of shear band formation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the processed (intervention) samples do not show statistically significant improvements in strain hardening behavior (i.e., increased uniform deformation before failure), reduced or delayed adiabatic shear band formation, and enhanced impact energy absorption compared to the baseline as-cast samples, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

For the W0 alloy, the yield strength (σYS) and the ultimate strength (σUS) are approximately 1620 MPa and 1810 MPa, respectively, with an elongation of ~22%. Serrated steps observed in the stress–strain curve of W0 suggest a susceptibility to plastic instability. The introduction of W into the alloy preserves the high yield strength while significantly improving both fracture strength and fracture strain []. For example, the W13 alloy demonstrates a yield strength of 1650 MPa, along with an ultimate strength of 2200 MPa and a fracture strain of 32%. Figure 2b presents the dynamic engineering stress–strain curves of alloys with varying W contents, tested at high strain rates (2000 s−1) and at room temperature. Under dynamic conditions, the yield strength of each alloy is significantly enhanced compared with the quasi-static conditions. Notably, while the W0 and W8 alloys exhibit poor dynamic plasticity with elongations below 10%, the W13 and W18 alloys demonstrate superior dynamic mechanical properties, achieving ultra-high dynamic yield strengths (exceeding 2200 MPa)

The engineering stress–strain curves of the W10 HEAs tested at room temperature under various strain rates (10−3, 1000, 2000, and 3000 s−1) are displayed in Figure 5a. Concurrently, the σYS and σUS values for both alloys under different conditions are summarized in Figure 5b. Under static compression conditions, the W10 alloy demonstrates a yield strength of 1490 MPa, along with an ultimate strength of 2200 MPa and a fracture strain of 30%. Compared to quasi-static conditions, the dynamic yield strength of the W10 alloy increases significantly from 1490 MPa to 2100 MPa when the strain rate increases to 1000 s−1 (Figure 5a). And the W10 alloy achieves an ultimate strength of 2300 MPa at 3000 s−1. The change in ultimate strength with the strain rate is less than 10%, showing minimal strain rate dependence (Figure 5b). AbstractThis paper investigates the effect of strain rate on the mechanical deformation and microstructural development of dual-phase AlCrFe2Ni2 high-entropy alloy during quasi-static and dynamic compression processes. It is revealed that the as-cast AlCrFe2Ni2 alloy is composed of a mixture of FCC, disordered BCC, and ordered B2 crystal structure phases. The alloy shows excellent compressive properties under quasi-static and dynamic deformation. The yield strength exceeds 600 MPa while the compressive strength is more than 3000 MPa at the compression rates of 30% under quasi-static conditions. Under dynamic compression conditions, the ultimate compression stresses are 1522 MPa, 1816 MPa, and 1925 MPa with compression strains about 12.8%, 14.7%, and 18.2% at strain rates of 1300 s−1, 1700 s−1 and 2100 s−1, respectively. The dynamic yield strength is approximately linear with strain rate within the specified range and exhibit great sensitivity. chosen.why: This approach directly targets the reported performance limitations—limited strain hardening, poor uniform deformability, and early failure at high strain rates—by producing a microstructure with a bimodal grain distribution. Such a refined microstructure is expected to improve strain hardening, delay localization and dynamic recrystallization, and enhance impact energy absorption. Using established thermomechanical treatment methods and testing protocols aligns well with standard practices in refractory high-entropy alloy research, making this a plausible and testable experimental intervention.
